summary: Describes how to use the ChaCha20 stream cipher with the Poly1305 authenticator, combined as an AEAD algorithm, in IKEv2 and IPsec. This gives IPsec an encryption option that performs well on devices without hardware AES support.

plainLanguage.summary: This teaches a secret-code machine a new way to scramble and seal messages, one that works fast even on small gadgets.

questions: what is chacha20 poly1305 in ikev2
what is the chacha20 poly1305 nonce in esp
what is transform id 28 in ikev2
subtitle: How IPsec and IKEv2 use ChaCha20-Poly1305 as a standby cipher alongside AES.

tldr.problem: IPsec in practice relies on AES alone, since the only other widely supported cipher, 3DES, is much slower. If a weakness in AES were found, VPN users would have no practical fallback.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines how the AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 algorithm from RFC 7539 is used in ESP and IKEv2: a 256-bit key, a 96-bit nonce built from a 32-bit salt and a 64-bit IV, and a 16-octet tag.
tldr.outcome: IPsec gains a second, independent AEAD cipher identified by transform ID 28. The security of the scheme depends above all on never reusing a nonce under one key.

today: RFC 7634 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Standby Cipher
sections.content:
The RFC notes that AES has become the go-to encryption algorithm, including in IPsec VPNs. On most modern platforms AES is four to ten times as fast as 3DES, and 3DES uses a 64-bit block, which limits how much data can be encrypted before rekeying. That makes AES the only viable choice for IPsec.

The risk is that a future weakness in AES would leave VPN users with only the much slower 3DES, making reconfiguration infeasible. This document proposes the ChaCha20 stream cipher with the Poly1305 authenticator, as an AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data), to serve as the standby for ESP (RFC 4303) and IKEv2 (RFC 7296). The algorithms themselves are in RFC 7539; this RFC covers only the IPsec-specific parts.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone uses one kind of lock. If someone finds out how to pick it, there must be another kind ready to use, so this RFC adds a second kind.

sections.title: Keys, Nonce and Counter in ESP
sections.content:
Usage follows the AEAD construction in Section 2.8 of RFC 7539. The Initialization Vector (IV) is 64 bits and MUST be unique for each invocation under a security association, but need not be unpredictable. A counter or LFSR is RECOMMENDED. A fixed per-SA 32-bit salt is prepended to the IV to form the 96-bit nonce, and the salt is not sent in the ESP packet.

The encryption key is 256 bits. IKE produces KEYMAT, and 36 octets are requested for each ChaCha20-Poly1305 key: the first 32 octets are the key and the last 4 are the salt.

ChaCha20 takes a 256-bit key, a 96-bit nonce and a 32-bit Initial Block Counter. For ESP the counter starts at one, because block counter zero is reserved for generating the one-time Poly1305 key. The top 256 bits of the ChaCha20 output for counter zero are used as that Poly1305 key.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock needs a secret key and a fresh number for every message. The fresh number is built from a fixed part both sides know and a counter part that changes each time.

sections.title: Authentication Tag and ESP Packet
sections.content:
Poly1305 is run over the following, in order: the AAD, zero padding up to a multiple of 16 octets (4 or 8 octets depending on AAD length), the ciphertext, zero padding to a multiple of 16 octets, the AAD length as a 64-bit little-endian integer, and the ciphertext length as a 64-bit little-endian integer. The 128-bit output is the tag, and all 16 octets go into the packet as the Integrity Check Value.

The plaintext still carries a pad length octet and a Next Header octet, as RFC 4303 specifies, and padding aligns it to a multiple of 4 octets. The ESP IV field holds the final 64 bits of the nonce. If a counter generates the IVs, the final 32 bits of the IV equal the Sequence Number field.

The AAD is built like in RFC 4106. With 32-bit sequence numbers it is 8 octets: a 4-octet SPI followed by a 4-octet sequence number. With Extended Sequence Numbers it is 12 octets: the SPI plus an 8-octet big-endian sequence number.
sections.plainLanguage: After scrambling, the sender stamps a 16-byte seal over the message and its label. The receiver checks the seal and throws the message away if it does not match.

sections.title: Use and Negotiation in IKEv2
sections.content:
In IKEv2 the algorithm is used as an AEAD in the Encrypted Payload per RFC 5282. Keying material is derived as for ESP: 36 octets are requested for each of SK_ei and SK_er (32 of key, 4 of salt), and none for SK_ai and SK_ar. The 64-bit IV is sent explicitly in the payload. The sender SHOULD include no padding and set Pad Length to zero, while the receiver MUST accept any padding length. With no unencrypted payloads the AAD is 32 octets: 28 for the IKEv2 header plus 4 for the encrypted payload header.

To negotiate it, the SA payload transform substructure uses ENCR_CHACHA20_POLY1305 (28) as the ENCR (type 1) transform ID. As with other AEADs, INTEG (type 3) transforms MUST NOT be specified, or one INTEG transform MAY be included with value NONE (0).
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers start talking, they agree on which lock to use by number. This lock is number 28, and they do not need a separate seal-checker because the lock already seals.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ChaCha20 is designed to provide 256-bit security. Poly1305 is designed so forged messages are rejected with probability 1-(n/(2^102)) for a 16n-octet message, even after 2^64 legitimate messages, making it SUF-CMA.

The most important implementation concern is nonce uniqueness for a given key. Unpredictability is not needed, so counters and LFSRs are fine. Side channels are trivial to avoid for ChaCha20 but need care for Poly1305; see RFC 7539.

The salt is never sent on the wire, but the algorithm's security does not depend on its secrecy. Implementations that keep key material inside a security boundary MAY therefore export the salt, which helps when a library takes the nonce rather than the IV.
sections.plainLanguage: The one rule that matters is never to use the same fresh number twice with the same key. It is fine if others can guess the number.

items.title: Key
items.text: 256 bits, the first 32 octets of the 36 octets of KEYMAT.

items.title: Salt
items.text: 32 bits, the last 4 octets of KEYMAT, fixed per SA and not transmitted.

items.title: IV
items.text: 64 bits, unique per invocation and sent in the packet.

items.title: Nonce
items.text: 96 bits: the salt followed by the IV.

items.title: Tag
items.text: 16 octets of Poly1305 output, carried as the ICV.
